definition: Remove a need or prevent a difficulty from arising.
example: A clear agreement obviated further debate.
nuance: Often use “obviate the need for,” rather than “obviate against.”
prompt: A team automates a repetitive check.
options: Automation can obviate the need for daily manual checks.
Automation obviated the need by making manual checks mandatory.
The new process obviated work by doubling the required effort.
Obviate meant to describe the check in more detail.
reasons: Removing the need for manual work illustrates obviate.
Making checks mandatory creates a need.
Doubling required work does not remove it.
Description is not prevention or removal of a need.

practice.prompt: A town opens a footbridge across a river that people once crossed by ferry.
options: Closing the footbridge for repairs will obviate the need for extra ferry trips.
Bright paint will help the footbridge obviate itself to passing drivers.
The engineers chose to obviate against building the deck too close to the water.
The new footbridge should obviate the need for the slow ferry crossing.
reasons: Shutting the bridge creates more demand for ferries instead of making them unnecessary.
This treats the word as a verb form of obvious, but it does not mean make easy to see.
The verb takes a direct object; obviate against mixes it up with militate against.
The bridge makes the ferry unnecessary, so the need goes away before it comes up.
